Toxicity and biodegradation of two different hydrothermal liquefaction
process waters for anaerobic digestion and the effect of microaeration

A R T I C L E  I N F O                  A B S T R A C T

Keywords:                                     Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) can convert a considerable portion of the carbon in complex feedstocks into
Hydrothermal liquefaction process water             renewable bio-oil, but it also generates an aqueous phase (i.e., HTL process water) that retains >30% of the
Anaerobic digestion                              carbon from the HTL feedstock. Feeding HTL process water to anaerobic digestion (AD) is a promising approach
Microaeration                                                       for maximizing resource recovery, enabling the conversion of the retained carbon into biogas. However, variousToxicity                                                     toxic and poorly biodegradable compounds in the HTL process water make its treatment with AD challenging.Biodegradability
                                                     Presently, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We investigated the impact of HTL process water from
                                         two different feedstocks – a food-waste proxy (i.e., dog food, rich in proteins) and wheat straw (rich in ligno­
                                                      cellulose) – on the different trophic groups in the food web of AD. We found that methanogens, rather than
                                                 acidogens, were more severely inhibited by HTL process water. Comparative toxicity and biodegradability an­
                                                    alyses showed that wheat-straw process water had a higher methane potential of 189 ± 1.52 mL CH4/g COD than
                                                    that of food-waste process water with a potential of 130 ± 0.13 mL CH4/g COD, regardless of its higher toxicity
                                                    to acetoclastic methanogens. The use of microaeration-acclimated biomass improved the methane yields of food-
                                             waste process water by 38% compared to anaerobic biomass, even without oxygen addition. However, the use of
                                                 microaeration-acclimated biomass or microaeration was ineffective for wheat-straw process water. These find­
                                                   ings highlight the importance of feedstock-specific strategies to optimize AD for biogas production from HTL
                                                 process water.
